title: On the floor
lead: How the Court of Master Sommeliers wants wine set up, opened, poured, decanted, stored and paired, plus the basic math behind a wine program.

intro.title: WHAT LEVEL 1 ASKS
intro.text: The Level 1 exam has basic service and food-and-wine pairing questions. In class you watch formal still and sparkling service; you are not graded on doing it.

tiers.name: Temperatures
tiers.note: No need to memorize at Level 1

sections.name: Mise en place

lines.label: Before service
lines.text: Wine lists are clean, correct and easy to read. Glasses are spotless, free of odor, and polished with clean linen over steam.

lines.label: On the table
lines.text: Only glass stemware touches the tablecloth. Bottles, decanters and corks always sit on an underliner.

know: Glassware and service items come to the table on a tray lined with a napkin.
Serviettes are cotton or similar, so they soak up liquid, and are folded before service.
Bottles, decanters and corks go on an underliner, never straight on the tablecloth.
Wines are stored and served at the right temperature, using ice buckets or decanters when needed.

visuals.title: The sommelier's kit
visuals.note: Plus pressed, clean clothes, safe shoes, clean nails and no strong perfume.

sections.name: Still wine service

lines.label: The host
lines.text: The host is the person who orders the wine. Every drink is served from the guest's right.

lines.label: The pour
lines.text: Once the host approves, pour clockwise. A guest of honor is served first. Fill glasses up to half full, depending on the glass size.

know: Take the order from the host's right and repeat it back.
Cut the foil at or below the second lip, so wine can't drip behind it.
Pour the host a 1 to 1.5 oz taste, step back, and wait for approval.
Wipe the bottle after every pour, and ask before removing the cork.
A screwcap is not presented. A synthetic cork is treated like a natural cork.

items.name: Present
items.text: Label to the host; repeat the name and vintage

items.name: Cut and wipe
items.text: Foil cut below the second lip; wipe the cork top

items.name: Open
items.text: Cork out quietly; present it on an underliner, host's right

items.name: Taste
items.text: 1 to 1.5 oz for the host, then wait

items.name: Pour
items.text: Clockwise, guest of honor first; up to half full

sections.name: Sparkling wine service

lines.label: Set up
lines.text: Chill the bottle. Bring flutes or tulips, an ice bucket with stand, and two serviettes. The bucket goes to the host's right.

lines.label: Open
lines.text: Cut the foil at the bottom of the cage. Loosen the cage but leave it on. Twist the bottle, not the cork, and let the cork out quietly.

know: Never take the cage off before the cork. Keep a hand or thumb over the cage and cork the whole time.
Hold the bottle at 45 degrees, always pointed away from the guests.
Pour the host a 1 to 1.5 oz taste, just like still wine.
Fill glasses evenly, up to 3/4 full, in no more than two pours each.

items.name: HAND ON TOP
items.text: Serviette and hand over the cage and cork, always
Bottle tilted, pointed away from guests

items.name: TWIST THE BOTTLE
items.text: Not the cork. Release it quietly

items.name: 3/4 FULL
items.text: Two pours per glass, at most

sections.name: Decanting

lines.label: Why
lines.text: Old red wine is decanted to leave its sediment behind. Young Cabernet Sauvignon often benefits from decanting too.

lines.label: How
lines.text: Pour into the decanter in one smooth movement, with the bottle above a candle or flashlight. Stop when sediment reaches the shoulder.

know: Decanting is done on a gueridon (a side cart), rolled to the host's right.
Light the candle away from the table when you can.
Never look away from the bottle while decanting.
Pour the host a 1 to 1.5 oz taste from the decanter, then serve the table.

visuals.title: On the gueridon
visuals.note: Everything goes on the gueridon before it moves to the table.

sections.name: Glassware

lines.label: Placement
lines.text: Glasses go to the guest's right, keyed off the knife. Every guest's setup looks the same.

lines.label: Order
lines.text: Start with the host or the person to the host's left, then go clockwise.

know: Choose the right size and shape of glass for each wine.
Several glasses can sit in a line, diagonal, diamond or cluster, depending on table space.
A new wine's glass goes to the right of earlier glasses, so you never pour over stemware.
A second bottle of the same wine gets a fresh glass for the host's taste.

items.name: NEW WINE
items.text: To the right of the last glass

items.name: SECOND BOTTLE
items.text: A fresh tasting glass for the host

sections.name: Temperature and storage

lines.label: Serving
lines.text: The Court sets temperature ranges for its exams. They are guidelines: the wine style and the guest decide in the end.

lines.label: Storage
lines.text: Cellar wine at a constant 50-60°F (10-15°C). Keep it away from light, vibration, damp, heat, odors and pests.

know: Sparkling, light-bodied whites and sweet whites are served coldest: 42-50°F.
Full-bodied reds are served warmest: 58-65°F.
Cork-finished wines are stored on their side; spirits and fortified wines stand up.
Don't store wine upright for more than a few weeks.

visuals.title: Serving temperature · °F
visuals.note: The Court's exam guidelines. Level 1 does not ask you to memorize them.

visuals.title: Long-term storage
visuals.text: Keep it constant. The Court calls 50-60°F (10-15°C) ideal for cellaring wine.

sections.name: Food and wine pairing

lines.label: At Level 1
lines.text: The Court teaches the basic principles of food and wine pairing and the classic pairings. Both show up on the Level 1 exam.

lines.label: The main idea
lines.text: Match the wine's weight to the food. Full-bodied wines suit rich, intense dishes. Intense flavors can be too much for very delicate dishes.

know: Bold red wines go with beef and lamb.
Rich sweet wines go with dessert and foie gras.
High-acid, unoaked wines go with seafood, starters and salads.
Sancerre is a classic pairing with fresh goat cheese.
With dessert, the wine should be sweeter than the dish.

items.name: MATCH WEIGHT
items.text: Full-bodied wine with rich, intense food

sections.name: Business of the sommelier

lines.label: At Level 1
lines.text: The Court introduces the business side at Level 1 but does not test it. It is tested at the Certified level.

lines.label: The math
lines.text: Cost of goods sold (COGS) = beginning inventory + purchases - ending inventory. Cost % = COGS ÷ wine sales.

know: A 30% wine cost means $30 in product for every $100 the business earns.
Inventory is counted in dollars: last month's count is the beginning inventory, this month's is the ending inventory.
Pours per bottle depend on pour size: divide the ounces in the bottle by the ounces per pour.
A standard bottle is 750 ml, or 25.4 oz.

visuals.title: Bottle sizes
visuals.note: Pours per bottle = ounces in the bottle ÷ ounces per pour.

visuals.title: Wine cost
visuals.text: For every $100 of wine sold, $30 is what the wine cost the restaurant.

mixups.why: Still: up to half full, depending on the glass. Sparkling: up to 3/4 full, in no more than two pours.
A cork is presented on an underliner to the host's right. A screwcap goes in your pocket and is not presented.
Cork-finished table wine lies on its side. Spirits and fortified wines stand up.
COGS is dollars: (beginning inventory + purchases) - ending inventory. Cost % is COGS divided by wine sales.

facts.fact: CMS-A Hospitality & Service Standards are the basis for measuring candidates in CMS-A exams; they are formal and 'not appropriate for many restaurants'.

Required sommelier tools: 2 wine bottle openers, 2 pens, 1 pad of paper, 2 odorless lighters or matches. Appearance: pressed, cleaned attire with comfortable, safe shoes; clean fingernails; no excessive perfumes or odors.

Mise en place: wine lists clean, correct, current and easy to read; glassware clean, spotless, free of odor, polished with clean linen using steam; serviettes cotton or similar that do not repel water, folded before service; underliners, trays, ice buckets, stands and decanters clean and ready.
Glass stemware is the only thing to touch the tablecloth; bottles, decanters and corks are placed on an underliner. Glassware and service items are brought on a tray lined with a napkin.
Wines are stored and served at the correct temperature; methods include ice buckets and decanters.
Beverage service is always performed on the right side of the guest. The order is taken from the host's right and repeated. The host is the person who orders the wine.

Present the bottle and repeat name and vintage. Cut the foil at the second or lower lip to prevent wine dripping behind the foil. Wipe the cork top. Remove the cork with minimal movement and as quietly as possible. Wipe the bottle top; present the cork to the right of the host on an underliner.

Pour the host a 1-1.5 ounce taste, label facing the host; step back and wait for approval. Then serve clockwise; a guest of honor is served first; regardless of gender. Wipe the bottle after each pour. Ask to remove the cork.
Glassware placement starts with the host or the person to the host's left and continues clockwise.

Glassware: right size and shape for each wine; placed to the guest's right, keyed off the knife; line, diagonal, diamond or cluster depending on space; consistent for all guests; second bottle of the same wine gets a fresh glass for the host's taste; new wine glasses go to the right of previous glasses so the sommelier does not pour over stemware.

Sparkling: prepare glassware (tulips or flutes), ice bucket, stand and two serviettes; bottle properly chilled; bucket to the host's right. Cut the foil at the bottom of the cage. Keep a serviette and hand or thumb over cage and cork; never remove the cage; point the bottle away from guests; twist the bottle, not the cork, at 45 degrees; release as quietly as possible; remove the cage from the cork afterwards.
Sparkling: pour a 1-1.5 ounce taste; fill glasses evenly up to 3/4 full, one glass at a time, maximum two pours per glass.
White and young red wine: glasses filled up to 1/2 full depending on the size of the stemware.

Decanting items: clean decanter, matches or odorless lighter, three serviettes, three underliners for the cork, bottle and decanter, candle or small flashlight, cork removal tools, decanting basket. A gueridon is used; all materials placed on it before moving tableside; roll it to the table, preferably to the host's right. Light the candle away from the table whenever possible.

Decanting: pour slowly into the decanter in one smooth movement, bottle a safe distance above the flame; use the candle or flashlight to look for sediment at the shoulder; never look away from the bottle; stop when sediment reaches the shoulder. Pour the host a 1-1.5 ounce taste from the decanter, then serve guests.

Storage: constant temperature; 50-60°F / 10-15°C ideal for long-term storage; away from odors and pests; cork-finished table wines on their side; spirits and fortified wines standing up; avoid direct light, vibration, overly damp conditions, storing upright for over a few weeks, excessive heat or temperature swings.
Screwcap: removed quietly and placed in the sommelier's pocket; not presented. Synthetic corks are treated the same as natural corks.

Suggested serving temperatures are guidelines; wine styles and consumer preference ultimately dictate. Exam standards: Champagne and sparkling 42-50°F; light-bodied white 42-50°F; sweet white 42-50°F; dry rosé 45-55°F; full-bodied white 50-59°F; light-bodied red 50-59°F; medium-bodied red 55-62°F; full-bodied red 58-65°F.
Learning objectives include an introduction to service by observing formal still and sparkling service by the bottle, and the basic principles of food and beverage pairing.

Sommelier Skills: Deductive Tasting Method intro and Business of the Sommelier intro are 'Not tested at this level'; Food and Beverage Pairing has a section quiz; Hospitality and Service uses the Service Standards in the workbook.
Exam content includes wine and food pairing (principles and interactions; classic pairings) and basic beverage service questions. 'No need to memorize service temperatures at this time.'
Practice exam question 38: classic pairing with fresh goat cheese; options Barolo, 10-Year Tawny Port, Sancerre, Napa Valley Cabernet Sauvignon; answer key: C (Sancerre).
Curriculum guide, Bordeaux, Introductory column: bold red wines with beef and lamb, rich sweet wines with dessert and foie gras.

Curriculum guide, California North Coast, Introductory column: young Cabernet Sauvignon often benefits from decanting; old Cabernet Sauvignon needs decanting for sediment; match full-bodied wines with food richness and intensity.
Curriculum guide, New Zealand, Introductory column: high-acid and unoaked wines with seafood, starters, salads; intense flavors can be too much for super delicate dishes.
Curriculum guide, Champagne, Certified column: Champagne is an incredibly versatile beverage that goes with many types of foods.
Curriculum guide, Piedmont, Certified column: big tannins require meat or fat.
Curriculum guide, Sweet Wines, Certified column: match the weight of the dessert and the wine; the wine should be sweeter than the dessert.
Curriculum guide, Hungary: Tokaji bottles are normally 500ml (17oz).

Business of the Sommelier is tested in the Certified theory exam. A 30% wine cost means for every $100 of revenue, $30 is product cost. Bottle sizes: half bottle 12.7 oz / 375 ml; standard 25.4 oz / 750 ml; magnum 50.7 oz / 1500 ml / 1.5 L. Understand how pour size relates to servings per bottle. COGS = (BI + P) - EI, with BI last month's inventory and EI this month's inventory in dollars. Cost % = COGS ÷ wine sales.

unverified: Level placement of some pairing rules: 'big tannins require meat or fat', 'the wine should be sweeter than the dessert' and 'Champagne goes with many types of food' sit in the Certified column of the Court's joint Introductory/Certified curriculum guide (column read from the PDF layout). The Court's Level 1 pairing chapter is in the Introductory workbook, which is only given to enrolled students and was not checked.

Standard by-the-glass pour for still wine: the Court gives no standard size. Its costing example uses 5 pours per bottle; the curriculum guide gives 2 oz for sweet and fortified wine by the glass (and lists 2 oz as both 59.1 ml and 51.9 ml). Not used in this chapter.
The magnum card's '3 liters (101.4 oz)' is a wrong-answer option only; the Court lists no bottle larger than a magnum.
